Austin.
Special to the Herald.
Austin, July 80.—The East Texas railroad
company presented amendments to their
charter to day, as follows: First, changing
the name of the company to the Sabine &
East Texas railroad company. Second, for
the construction of a branch line from a
point in Nacogdoches county to a point on
the Sabine river, opposite or nearly opposite
Logansport, La.
A report reached here to-day that a deputy
sheriff of Hayes county, yesterday, shot and
killed a negro for resisting arrest. The kill-
ing occurred near the railroad bridge on the
Blanco river. The names of the parties are
not known.
Yesterday evening Julius Loeschmann, a well known citizen of Austin, was found dead in his tent in the cedar brake, about ten miles from the city, where he had been in charge of a wood camp. A doubled barrelled shot gun with one barrel discharged, was found on the ground beside the remains. There was a hole in the right temple. A jury of inquest to-day returned a verdict of death from accidental shooting.

Constable Kroose to-day arrested one George Thomas, accused of cattle stealing in Hayes county. He will have a hearing on Monday.

The veteran claims recommended to-day were as follows: Juana N Alsbury, L C Dumbough, B F Foster, Richard Douglass, Annie M Bryan, James Dever, Joseph Burleson, Clemente Bustillo, Caroline Banan, Julia A Eggleston, A Parker, A C Delaplain, M G. Whitaker, Eliza Hubble, Melinda Magee, George Brooks, W. R. Newman and Mary Caruthers.

The first number of the Austin Citizen, a republican paper, edited by a colored man, made its appearance to-day.

The report has come here by private letter, of the burning to death at Lockhart of Viola Franklin, a little girl. by a coal oil lamp explosion.
The school board met this evening and appointed Professor Pritchell, of San Marcos, assistant to Professor Baldwin, of the Sam Houston Normal school.

Ex-Senator Conkling says he intends to practice "a little law" in this country if he can get the permission of the editors who have been opposing his re-election; that he would not presume to practice without this permission. This little bit of irony indicates that the Senator thinks it was the newspapers that killed him. He is mistaken. It was a case of suicide.

The Abbeville Median says: "The young ladies of Greenwood mean business. They give no countenance to a young man who drinks liquor, and will give him no show in the reading club, upon the ground that liquor and learning don't go well together. A number of the young men have succumbed, for they prefer the smiles of a charming young lady to a good drink of whiskey."

The bonanza kings of the Pacific coast keep accumulating wealth, while the individual stockholders of their mining property are assessed out of existence. The tax rolls of San Francisco give the personal property of a few of them as follows: James G. Fair, United States Senator from Nevada, $42,200,000; J. C. Flood, $33,500,000; J. W. Mackey, $20,500,000; Charles Crocker, $20,000,000.

A negro man named Jim Goode, living on Mr. Samuel Cathecart's plantation in Fairfield County, was severely burned on Friday night last, and died from his injuries on Saturday morning. He had a kerosene lamp in his room, and undertook to till it while it was lighted. The oil in the can became ignited, and, the can exploding, the burning liquid was thrown on the clothing of the man.

A dispatch to the News and Courier, from Laurens, S. C., dated July 25, says: "A negro man was shot and killed by his brother on yesterday, on the plantation of Mr. J. R. Fowler, living in the neighborhood of Warner's Creek Church. It appears that the deceased had been beating his wife unmercifully, and was ordered to stop by his brother, but on refusing to desist the brother blew out his brains with a musket."

There is a gospel "boom" going on among the deps and dives of New York. Miss Minnie Brooks was first converted from the evil of her ways, and turned her house into a mission meeting place. She sold her furniture and finery, and is resolved to devote herself henceforth and forever to the reforming of her class. She has been joined by several Christian workers, and many of the wild and wayward young girls of the neighborhood are following in the footsteps of Minnie to a better life.

The Williamsburg Herald says: The sheriff attempted to arrest Jack Hicks, a colored man, last Monday morning. No sooner did the sheriff order him to surrender than he ran off, when the sheriff fired four shots, two of which took effect, one in his shoulder, just above the blade, and the other in the leg. He made good his escape, but it is thought he will die. There were three indictments out for him, one for stealing cotton, one for breaking jail and turning out prisoners, and another for not paying his poll tax.

The administration of the Postoffice Department upon business principles has already reduced the expenses about $2,000,000 per annum without in any manner impairing the efficiency of the service. Meantime the receipts are steadily increasing, and it is not improbable that the Department by the end of the fiscal year will become self-supporting. The next step of the government then, no doubt, will be to cheapen the postal service. A reduction upon letter postage and of the cost of money orders would be acceptable to the people.

On last last Wednesday night the barn and stables of Mr. R. J. Gladney, in Fairfield County, were destroyed by an incendiary fire. The barn was a two story building, and the stalls for the live stock surrounded the lower story. The
The Beaufort Crescent, of July 28, says: "The family of Mr. John Barnwell were taken suddenly ill on Sunday evening, and Dr. Stuart on being summoned found symptoms of poisoning. There were nine persons affected, and for a time several of them were in a critical condition. The Doctor administered antidotes for tartar emetic and the patients were soon relieved. The poisoning was owing to one of two causes, watermelon or canned beef; but as the melon came from Augusta the Doctor inclines to the opinion that it resulted from some impurity in the beef. A rather significant fact, however, occurred yesterday. A colored man attempted to purchase tartar emetic to 'fix' his watermelons, as they were disappearing too fast."

The scarlet fever seems to have broken out more violently than ever in seaside costumes this year. Unshaded red in parasols, hat linings, and yatching and bathing suits is universally worn, and the eye fairly aches for more subdued and harmonious tones on beach and esplanade, where the unmerciful rays of the summer sun beat down upon whole forests of female forms, every one of which displays some garment or ribbon of this florid and glaring hue, and the combinations occasionally to be seen with other colors seem only intended to bring out the favorite scarlet in stronger relief and with greater violence. Red with purple facings, saffron with scarlet stripes, rich cardinal with black trimmings, in true Mephistophelian style, are worn by matrons and maidens without any reference whatever to age, complexion, or becomingness.
— A twelve-year old son of Mr. Eli Moore, of Darlington county, came to his death in a mysterious manner last week. He went out to the field to carry water to his father as usual, and not coming on time the father became uncasy and instituted a search for his son, whose clothing was found on the bank of Lynch's River. The river was dragged and the body was found about fifty yards from where the clothing was found. The boy's neck was broken. An inquest was held by Trial Justice Fountain. Dr. Palmer, who held the post mortem examination, said the boy came to his death by his neck being broken; he did not die. The manner in which his neck was broken would have caused respiration to have ceased almost immediately. The jury returned a verdict "that the deceased was found in Lynch's River with his neck broken by some cause, mischance or accident, entirely unknown to the jury."

A Small Insurrection.
Hot Springs, July 8.—At a negro barbecue here Wednesday a quarrel began, and the trial was let for yesterday. The court room was early surrounded by two hundred or more negroes, mostly armed with guns. Officers arrested one of them for drunkenness, and the negroes evinced a determination to take him away instantly. Four or five hundred armed whites appeared on the streets and protected the officers. No further trouble is expected.

CRIMES AND CASUALTIES
An Oil-Laden English Bark Destroyed by Lightning—One Sailor Drowned and the Captain and Others of the Crew Injured—Four People Killed and Eight Injured by Lightning near Decatur, Ala.—Desperate Fight Between Whites and Blacks in Arkansas—Cattle Fire at Buffalo, N. Y.

STRUCK AND BURNED BY LIGHTNING.

PHILADELPHIA, July 8.—The British bark Beatrice, Captain Stewart, for Rover, with oil, was struck by lightning while off Reedy Island. The fluid ran down the main mast into the hold, and fired the cargo. An explosion followed, and the main hatch was blown into the river, and a sailor with it, who was drowned. Captain Stewart, the mate and two sailors were injured by flying timbers. The vessel burned to the water's edge.

A PLUCKY WIFE.

MANCHESTER, N. H., July 8.—Two burglars, giving the names of Thomas Callahan and Dominick Moran, were discovered at Piscassaquog early this morning in the bedroom of F. Hutchinson, rifling his pockets. Hutchinson seized Callahan and in the struggle both fell down stairs. Mrs. Hutchinson, with a revolver, ran to the aid of her husband, pounding the burglar's head and face severely, and enabled her husband to secure him. He then telephoned the police, who jailed the burglar, and pursued and captured Moran.

RACE CONFLICT IN ARKANSAS.

LITTLE ROCK, July 8.—Intelligence reached here this morning of a serious disturbance at Mineral Springs, Howard county. Wednesday the negroes had a barbecue near town. In the evening they flocked to the Springs in large numbers.
Two who became involved in a quarrel were arrested therefor. At an early hour yesterday the trial began, and the negroes began to congregate, each with a musket or shotgun. By 10 o'clock 200 or more were in town, nearly all of whom were armed. The white citizens, fearing trouble, prepared their guns and placed them in convenient places. At 1 o'clock one negro was arrested for drunkenness and disorderly conduct, when the negroes showed a determination to take him from the officers, and a riot occurred. Almost instantly forty or fifty white men were on the streets with guns. Fortunately no one was hurt. One or two shots were accidentally fired in the air. A number negroes were arrested. Matters are now quiet, but further trouble is apprehended.

HANGED.

NEW ORLEANS, July 8.—Samuel Trivias was hanged this morning in Alexandria, Rapid parish, for the murder of A. J. Hanna.

KILLED BY LIGHTNING.

DECATUR, Ala., July 8.—During a thunderstorm last evening lightning struck a barn where a number of people had sought refuge, and four were killed and eight seriously injured.

CATTLE BURNED.

BUFFALO, July 8.—The large feeding barns of J. Firmenich, near the stock yards, containing about 800 cattle, burned. Three hundred and sixty-two cattle perished. Loss $28,000; insured.

Appleton, the publisher, died Thursday.
Guitteau, for a time, sojourned in the Oneida community.
The Lafayette family sent condolences from Paris to Washington.
Nine miles of the Yale & Sabona R. R., British Columbia, have been laid.
Guitteau wants his biography written, and says it would read like a romance.
A sanguinary squabble occurred at a negro barbecue near Mineral Springs, Ark.
Griscom, the Chicago faster, has gone to eating again and has an accelerated appetite.
There were twenty cases of sunstroke in Cincinninnati and eleven in Covington on the 10th.
It is reported that Conkling has expressed a firm determination to remain in Senatorial fight.
The Oberammergau Passion players failed in their attempt at performing a secular drama.

Prof. Riley has been appointed entomologist of the Agricultural Bureau, vice Comstock, resigned.

Dr. Hamilton says the symptoms in Garfield's case indicate that nature will take care of the ball.

The Liberte and National, of Paris, advise the British Government to "mind their own business."

The wife and three daughters of the English Mayor General Fyers were drowned at Hyeres, France.

Four hundred head of cattle perished with the burning of the large feeding barns of J. Firemich, at Buffalo.

At a caucus of the Republican members of the New York Legislature, Miller and Lapham were nominated.

Hon. Phineas W. Hitchcock, ex-United States Senator from Nebraska, died at his home in Omaha on the 10th.

A French company with $10,000,000 capital is being formed in Paris to develop the mining resources of Canada.

The thermometer indicated 104 at Cincinnati Wednesday. Thirteen cases of sunstroke, mostly fatal, were reported.

For stock operations a bogus report was circulated, on Friday, that second hemorrhage had set in, in the President's case.

Siemens Bros., who have just finished the new Atlantic cable, send as the first message a congratulation to the President.

The people of Freeport, Ill., deeply realize the odium resting on their town on account of Guittteau's former residence there.

The deputation of Irish farm laborers, sent to London, was accompanied on their visit to Foster by eighty member's of Parliament.

Work on the Hudson river tunnel now extends about 300 feet from the Jersey shore, and the tunnel is to be completed in three years.

The British steamer Oceanic, from Hongkong via Yokohoma, arrived in San Francisco last Sunday with 1,000 Chinese on board.

The thermometer has marked from 96 to 98 daily for over a week at Memphis. There were five fatal cases of sunstroke there last Sunday.

The Republicans of San Francisco have nominated ex-County Judge M. C. Blake for Mayor, and ex-Revenue Collector John Sedgwick for Sheriff.

In Joint Convention at Albany last Saturday the ballot of the short term, combined, was: Potter 50, Conkling 31, Lapham 67, Wheeler 1. No Choice.

J. S. Morton, Jno. H. Dean, Moses Taylor and C. F. Woerishoffer, of New York, each subscribed $5,000 to the Mrs. Garfield fund, which now amounts to $75,000.

Lefroy, charged with the murder of Golde on the Brighton Railroad on the 27th of June, has been arrested at East London, and made a full confession of committing the crime.

One of Guitteau's letters, now in possession of the District Attorney, reflects bitterly upon Blaine and leads to the inference that Guitteau entertained designs upon the life of the Secretary.

The Governor, Secretary of State and Treasurer of Oregon unite in a dispatch to Blaine, congratulating him on behalf of the people of Oregon on the improving prospects of the President.

Director of the Mint Bureau, Burchard, left Washington Monday to be absent two months. He will visit San Francisco and the Territories for the purpose of collecting statistics of the product of gold and silver.

Many incidents are being reported by letter writers which point to the fact that Guitteau had accomplices in his crime. The prisoner is closely guarded and kept ignorant of everything transpiring outside of his cell.

The Governors of all the States and Territories have responded to Governor Foster's telegram, and agree as to the propriety of a national thanksgiving day for the President's recovery, as soon as he is out of danger.

Monday the facts came out in regard to the difficulty which occurred among the physicians in attendance upon President Garfield at the time Dr. J. H. Baxter made his attempt to gain admission as one of the consulting physicians. Dr. Bliss was very plain in his language to Baxter, saying he was nothing but a professional lobbyist, seeking the position of Surgeon General.
A Chicago dispatch says: The passenger war, has broken out in the east on west bound traffic, although not quite so open here, is none the less hot and determined. One general passenger agent of a prominent line said it was useless to deny facts which the world will know to-morrow, that passenger rates are being furiously cut, and it will be a question soon of how much money the applicant has got and not what the good can get.

LYNCHING OF THE TETON MURDER. ER.
Particulars of his Fiendish Crime.
On Friday evening, July 1st, a party of masked men rode up to Mr. A. B. Hamilton, who was bringing to Benton the man, Brackett E. Stewart, who was charged with the murder of Mrs. Armstrong and O. H. Morgan, leveled their guns at him, and demanded his prisoner. These men were immediately after joined by about twenty more, and they took the prisoner by force from Mr. Hamilton, and hung him to a tree near Hamilton & Hazlett's place at Old Agency. He exhibited no emotion, but appeared entirely indifferent in regard to his approaching end, and only requested the avenging party to
tom-stewart-old-agency-1881-07-01.A3:
be sure and break his neck. The above facts were sworn to by Mr. Hamilton at the coroner's inquest held over the body of Stewart and before Judge Tattan. Mr. Hamilton swore that he did not recognize any of the party, and would not be able to identify any of them, and the coroner's jury brought in a verdict that Stewart "came to his death by hanging; that said hanging was committed by persons to the jury unknown." And so closed the earthly career of the perpetrator of one of the most fiendish and deliberate murders that disgrace the history of our Territory, the particulars of which, as gathered from the deposition of witnesses, are as follows:

Stewart came to Morgan's ranch two days before the murder. He told Morgan something about horses, and he and Morgan went out that day looking for horses. The next day he stayed around the house, evidently preparing the robbery and murder. It is not known whether he slept up stairs with Morgan the night preceding the murder, or whether he slept in the stable where he stayed the first night. Morgan slept up stairs, the steps leading to his room being on the outside of the house, and Mrs. Armstrong occupied a room down stairs, in which also were Maggie Houseman, a little girl of 12, and Annie Keogh, aged 6. The murderer first shot Morgan, the report of the gun waking Mrs. Armstrong, who asked, "What is that!" Stewart, who by this time must have come down stairs, said it was a coyote among the turkeys. Mrs. Armstrong told Maggie to get up and look after the turkeys. When Maggie got outside she saw Stewart with a gun, and asked him not to kill her, to which he answered "oh, no." When she returned he stood at the door of Mrs. Armstrong's room, with a gun in his hand. He fired two shots, the bullets striking Mrs. Armstrong behind the right shoulder. Maggie ran away then, but came back to get Annie Keogh, and at that time Mrs. Armstrong was lying in the sitting room, dead, and the murderer was going through the trunks and boxes. The little girl went upstairs and saw Morgan lying in bed, his mouth open and his eyes partly open and apparently dead. She got afraid and took Annie and ran to the brush opposite the house. While they were in the brush they saw the house burning, and saw a mare near by, and Maggie went back to the house and got a saddle, which she put on the mare, and her and Annie rode toward H. L. Kennerly's and on the way met that gentleman and told him of the murder. This was the substance of Maggie Housman's testimony, which was corroborated by Annie Keogh.

From the description given by the little girl Mr. Kennerly recognized Stewart as the man, and he and Mr. Hamilton arrested Stewart. Stewart was standing in front of the store with about fifteen other men, and was immediately recognized and singled out from the others by Maggie, and was also identified by Annie. A pair of blankets then in the possession of Stewart, and which he had not had a few days before, were proved to have belonged to Mrs. Armstrong.

There is no doubt, from the corroborative evidence, that Stewart was the murderer, and though lynch law is to be deprecated, the community will hardly find fault with the swift retribution meted out to the fiend in human shape who could thus deliberately commit such an atrocious crime for motives of gain, and the prompt punishment will go far toward preventing a similar crime.

[SPECIAL TO THE HERALD.] Fort Shaw, June 30. O. H. Morgan and Mrs. Annie Armstrong were murdered in their house near the mouth of the Muddy, on the Teton, yesterday morn-1 ing about five o'clock, aud the house and bodies burned. Two little girls living with Mrs. Armstrong escaped and hid in the brush. The eldest, about twelve years old, says a man came there early in the morning and 1 illed her mother and Mr. Morgan, and then searched all the trunks for money, and then set fire to the house. A man has been ar rested on suspicion, and all circumstances seem to indicate that he is the person who committed the horrible crime. F. G. HELOT. Commencement of St. V incent's Acad emy. News From Old Agency,
Mr. H. Brinkman returned from the Old Agency on Tuesday with twenty-seven head of horses. He tells us that everything is prosperous in that section and that the residents are in unusually good spirits. Mr. Brinkman arrived at Old Agency in time to assist in the burial of Morgan and Mrs. Armstrong, the victims of the fiend Stewart. The sad work of interment was performed by A. B. Hamilton and Mr. Brinkman. The latter saw also the place where Stewart was strung up and the grave in which his remains lie, not very deep down either. When the lynching job was well finished each of the men engaged in the work took a piece of the rope as a relic and the various articles he had on his person were also distributed among the committee as reminders of the deed they had done.

The cow boys will finish the round up in about eight days. The losses are very light.

Mr. Hamilton has plenty of nice, ripe strawberries and on the 4th of August he proposes to give a grand festival or strawberry treat. The editor has been invited to assist in the work of demolishing the luscious berry, and he would certainly be pleased to do so if the long distance did not intervene.
